title: Spatial structure of land value potential after land consolidation using spatial econometric modelling — Mevlüt Uyan, Land Use Policy (Elsevier) vol. 172, article 108343, online 16 September 2026 (print issue dated January 2027)
what_was_fetched: Abstract, four 'Highlights' bullets, keywords and the 45-item reference list only. Full text NOT read. Route: doi.org redirects to ScienceDirect (pii S0264837726004278); ScienceDirect HTML and /pdf return HTTP 403 (bot challenge) to curl with a browser user-agent and to r.jina.ai; r.jina.ai did return the ScienceDirect landing page text (abstract + highlights + 'Data availability: Data will be made available on request'). Crossref API gave metadata and the full reference list (no abstract); OpenAlex gave the abstract (inverted index), the author's institution and publication record; Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall both list a hybrid open-access CC BY-NC-ND copy but only at the same blocked ScienceDirect PDF URL (no repository or author copy exists: OpenAlex any_repository_has_fulltext = false). Not tried successfully: ResearchGate or a Konya Technical University repository copy (none indexed). Saved under t0-2026-10-12: crossref.json, openalex.json, uyan_author.json, uyan_jina.txt (landing-page text), uyan.pdf (this is the 403 challenge page, not the paper).
verdict: REJECT. Abstract-only, and the abstract is thin for the wiki's purposes: the paper measures an agricultural-consolidation outcome index, not a market price or a rent, and says nothing (in the part visible) about taxing, recovering or distributing the uplift. Re-open only if an editor with full-text access finds explicit valuation-method or uplift-distribution content; even then the sole plausible home is one clause in the Turkey paragraph of research/mass-appraisal-international-cases.md, not a new page (no concept page for 'agricultural land consolidation' exists and the paper is not land pooling / readjustment in the urban betterment sense).
claim_grade: C (abstract-level empirical claim; method and data unverified) — source tier under §4c: Tier 1-eligible venue (peer-reviewed Elsevier journal, Land Use Policy, ABDC-A) and a working academic author (see uncertainties), but the wiki can only cite the abstract. Nothing in it supports a Georgist claim.

content_summary.study_area_and_data: One agricultural land-consolidation (LC) project in Türkiye (province and village not named in the abstract or highlights); parcel-level data before and after consolidation. Number of parcels not stated in the visible text. Data 'will be made available on request'.
content_summary.land_value_potential_measure: Highlights: 'A novel Land Value Potential (LVP) indicator is operationalised for evaluating land consolidation outcomes.' The abstract reports LVP as a unit-less index (mean 0.491 before, 0.737 after), so it is a normalised score, not a currency value. How it is built is not visible; the reference list (Ertunç 2022, 'Land valuation with best worst method in land consolidation projects', Land Use Policy; Rezaei 2015, 'Best-worst multi-criteria decision-making method', Omega) suggests a multi-criteria weighting approach — an inference from the bibliography, not a stated fact.
content_summary.method: Explanatory variables: change in parcel compactness (ΔCI; reference list includes Polsby 1991 on compactness), fragmentation, and pre-consolidation LVP. OLS compared with spatial lag (SAR) and Spatial Error Model (SEM). Reference list includes Anselin 1988, Elhorst 2014, Bidanset 2014 (GWR vs spatial lag in mass real-estate appraisal) and Demetriou 2017 (spatial ANN mass valuation model for land consolidation).
content_summary.findings_with_figures: Mean LVP rose from 0.491 to 0.737, 'approximately 50%'. OLS residuals show significant spatial autocorrelation: Moran's I = 0.198, p < 0.001. SEM selected on AIC = -510.51 (SEM beats OLS and SAR per the highlights). Interpretation: post-consolidation LVP is driven by 'spatially structured contextual factors rather than direct parcel-to-parcel interactions'; LC 'reshapes rather than eliminates inherited spatial value structures'. Highlight 4: 'Land consolidation reshapes parcel structure but does not eliminate spatially embedded value inequalities.' Coefficients, R-squared, parcel count and per-variable effects are not in the visible text.
content_summary.who_captures_the_uplift: Not addressed in the abstract or highlights. No mention of landowner shares, state cost recovery, betterment charges, taxes or beneficiaries. The closest statement is the abstract's closing aim of 'more robust and equitable evaluations of LC programmes' and the highlight on 'spatially embedded value inequalities' — i.e. an equity-of-outcome framing between parcels, not a capture-of-uplift framing.
content_summary.author_standing_rubric: Mevlüt Uyan: Konya Technical University, Vocational School of Technical Sciences, Konya, Türkiye (OpenAlex/Crossref affiliation; ORCID 0000-0002-3415-6893). OpenAlex author record: 44 works, about 1,600 citations, h-index 17; topics soil/land suitability, multi-criteria decision-making, land rights and reforms. His own prior work in this paper's reference list: Uyan 2020, 'Comparison of different optimization based land reallocation models' (Computers and Electronics in Agriculture) and Uyan 2025, carbon footprint in land consolidation (same journal). Under the §4c rubric: an established academic with a peer-reviewed record in land consolidation / reallocation, publishing in a high-ranked journal — Tier 1-eligible on his own field (consolidation methods), not a Georgist or land-tax authority. Not on sources/audit/people-tiers.json.
content_summary.quote_locators: No quotations taken from the full text. Abstract and Highlights as reproduced above are on the ScienceDirect landing page (pii S0264837726004278).

existing_wiki_coverage: research/mass-appraisal-international-cases.md already carries two land-consolidation valuation cases: Kilić, Rogulj & Jajac (2019, Hvar, Croatia; fuzzy expert system for land valuation in consolidation, abstract-level) and Yalpır & Ünel (2017, Konya, Türkiye; GIS plus multiple regression, R-squared 0.85, MAPE about 29%, full text read). Yalpır & Ünel is also a Konya study, so Uyan extends the same Turkish region and the same consolidation-valuation line, but with an index (not market-price) outcome. concepts/land-pooling.md covers urban land readjustment (Gujarat TPS, Sanyal & Deuskar) and does not discuss agricultural consolidation; it links land-value-capture, betterment-levy, singapore, tideman-plassmann-land-assembly. concepts/mass-appraisal-methods.md has no spatial-error or SEM discussion in the digest. No page covers Uyan or Land Use Policy 2026.
uncertainties: Full text unread: project location, parcel count, how LVP is constructed (market data vs expert/MCDM weights), and whether the paper discusses landowner compensation, cost recovery or inequality between owners are all unknown.
The abstract's 'approximately 50%' LVP improvement is a change in an index, so it must not be reported as a 50% rise in land price or rent.
Crossref lists a print date of January 2027 (vol. 172) and Elsevier calls the page 'in press'/complimentary access; citation details may change.
Whether the open-access PDF is genuinely CC BY-NC-ND is taken from OpenAlex and Unpaywall metadata; not verified on the publisher page.

title: Enduring But Unacknowledged: The Georgist Inheritance in Australia — text by Phil Day (1924-2011); posted by Bryan Kavanagh (site author account) on thedepression.org.au ('Fixing The Depression We Had To Have'), 14 September 2026
what_was_fetched: Full essay, read end to end (about 64,700 characters of text including Appendix A and the reference list), fetched with curl and a browser user-agent (HTTP 200); no paywall. Saved as depression.html and depression.txt. Also fetched: Wikipedia 'Phil Day (town planner)' (raw wikitext), Wikipedia 'Rae Else-Mitchell' and 'Leonie Sandercock' (raw), Treasury 'A brief history of Australia's tax system' (Economic Roundup Winter 2006), ADB entries for Griffith and Else-Mitchell (no hits on the Natural Law Bill). NOT reachable: the NSW Parliamentary Library 'Land Tax: An Update' PDF (HTTP 403), AustLII Mabo and Wik judgments (HTTP 403), the KIT library catalogue entry that lists the essay's title as a book chapter (connection reset). Not read: Day 1995 and 2007, Hutchinson 1979, Else-Mitchell 1974, Sandercock 1975/1979, Jupp 1997 (books; none online). Primary sources the essay cites (Queensland Hansard 1890, the 1967 NSW Royal Commission report, Brisbane City Council 1989 report, the 1973 Land Tenures report, Bingham v Cumberland County Council 1954) were not located online.
verdict: ENRICH, narrowly; no NEW page. (1) places/australia.md: add a short historiography paragraph (colonial antecedents; Day's reading that Australian land taxation was never explicitly Georgist) anchored on Treasury 2006 and the Else-Mitchell/Roberts scholarship, with Day cited as a labelled Tier 2 commentator. (2) concepts/betterment-levy.md: one sentence on the 1971-73 NSW Green Belt levy and the ACT 1971 levy, only if a Tier 1 source (1967 Royal Commission report or Archer 1976) is located; otherwise hold. (3) people/bryan-kavanagh.md and organizations/prosper-australia.md: two small corroborating facts. Do NOT create research/ page on the essay (Tier 2 origin material, dated c.2005, little that is new and Tier 1 anchored) and do NOT create people/phil-day.md now (see judgement below).
claim_grade: D (interpretive / argumentative overall) with A-claims where Day reports dated events and documents. Source tier under §4c: Tier 2 for Day (see standing) and Tier 2 for the host (Kavanagh is Tier 2 on people-tiers.json; he republishes rather than authors). The scholarship Day cites is mixed: Else-Mitchell (judge, royal commissioner, Commonwealth Grants Commission chair), S.H. Roberts, Cannon, Sandercock 1975, Mabo/Wik are Tier 1; Hutchinson 1979 (Land Values Research Group founder) and Jupp 1997 (Othila Press) are Tier 2 advocacy-body or practitioner works.

content_summary.authorship_and_dating_correction: The page byline reads 'Bryan Kavanagh' with 'Phil Day' beneath, and the queue item lists both as authors. The text is Day's alone: Kavanagh appears inside the essay in the third person ('respected valuer Bryan Kavanagh', section The Georgist Movement), and 'Bryan Kavanagh' is the site's default author account (?author=1). The essay is NOT new in 2026: internal evidence dates it to about 2004-05 (it cites a Courier Mail piece of 12.6.04, 'in 2004 interest in betterment and compensation resurfaced', the centenary of Progress 'in May, 2004', Stilwell 2000 as latest bibliography entry, 'at the time of writing' for Howard-era politics). It reads as a book chapter (it refers to 'Frank Stilwell's chapter', 'Terry Dwyer's chapter' and 'John Pullen'); the original publication was not located (a library catalogue snippet lists the title as chapter 11 of an unnamed multi-author Henry George volume — unverified). It therefore cannot speak to the Henry Review (2009-10), the ACT stamp-duty transition or any post-2005 event. It also does not mention the Torrens title system at all.
content_summary.standing_of_phil_day: Philip Denny Day (1924-17 March 2011): law graduate (UQ, 1953), ACT Advisory Council member 1955-59, trained in town and country planning, NSW Department of Decentralisation and Development director, Brisbane City Council director of town planning, University of Queensland (Department of Regional and Town Planning from 1974; head of school 1977-80), director of the Australian Institute of Urban Studies from 1980, member of the Brisbane Committee of Inquiry into Valuation and Rating (the 'Chalk Committee', report 1989 — the committee the essay describes without saying he sat on it), editor of Queensland Planner from 1987, PhD completed aged 77 (published as Hijacked Inheritance), books: Land Value Capture (Local Government Association of Queensland, 1992), Land: The Elusive Quest for Social Justice, Taxation Reform and a Sustainable Planetary Environment (Australian Academic Press, Brisbane, 1995; Wiley-Blackwell 2007 edition). Sources for this: Wikipedia 'Phil Day (town planner)' (itself citing a Courier-Mail obituary, 20 April 2011) and a Wiley author blurb found by search. Rubric judgement: he WAS an academic in the sense of a UQ head of school and later PhD, but his publication record located is two single-author books plus reports; no peer-reviewed article record on land taxation was found, and he was a practising planner, an inquiry member and a Georgist-sympathetic commentator. Tier 2 (practitioner-academic): origin and proponent of the reading; may be cited for his own description of events he took part in, and as a pointer to primaries, never as evidence that Georgist influence exists. Not on people-tiers.json; the list should record him as Tier 2 if this essay is used.
content_summary.structure: Sections in order: ORIGINS (1788 settlement, Cook's 1768 instructions, Roberts's History of Australian Land Settlement); EVOLUTION OF LAND LAW (quit-rents, squatting, Gipps and Wentworth, Earl Grey 1848, Mabo 1992 and Wik 1996, Else-Mitchell 1974, Melville, Gresham, Dutton, 1880s Melbourne speculation); THE COMMITMENT TO LEASEHOLD IN CANBERRA; LAND TAXES; SAMUEL GRIFFITH'S NATURAL LAW BILL (1890; text in Appendix A); TAX REFORM (1985 and 1996 tax summits, the LVRG 'Challenge', GST 2000); THE GEORGIST MOVEMENT; THE IMPACT OF TOWN PLANNING (1932 UK Act, Bingham 1954, 1967 NSW Royal Commission evidence, Day 1995); PRAGMATIC RESPONSES (developer contributions, NSW EP&A Act 1979, Brisbane 1989 committee, Vancouver Plan 1976, Very Fast Train 1990, Jubilee Line, Judge Foster 1947); BETTERMENT AND COMPENSATION (2004 Queensland vegetation clearing); ATTEMPTING AN ASSESSMENT; Appendix A (Griffith's Bill); References and Further Reading.

authors_own_georgist_reading_vs_document.documented_record: Dated events and documents: Canberra leasehold history; 1890 Griffith Bill; 1954 Bingham decision; ACT and NSW betterment levies; 1967 Royal Commission; developer-contribution practice; 1989 Brisbane inquiry; Australia's 1976 endorsement; the 1985 and 1996 tax summits.
authors_own_georgist_reading_vs_document.authors_reading: That these amount to a 'tangible and enduring' Georgist inheritance even though 'the Georgist influence is nowhere explicit'; that the fatal flaw of the planning system is private capture of public-decision windfalls; that land value taxation is the 'logically irrefutable' response; the closing moral claim about 'creeping dollar darwinism'. Day himself is more cautious than the queue summary implies: he concedes the 1910 tax and state taxes were not Georgist in rationale, that much practice is 'compatible with' rather than caused by Georgism, that the movement has been ineffective, and that the assessment 'must unavoidably be subjective'.

verdict: ENRICH concepts/land-value-capture.md with one new bullet on the Transbay case, carrying ICLEI only as a practitioner body's position, anchored on the FHWA profile and the SF Controller's memo, and set against Merriman's Tier 1 'TIF is not additional land value capture' finding. Optional second site: places/san-francisco.md (no Transbay content there today). Do NOT enrich research/uic-chicago-tif-who-paid-who-gained.md: the ICLEI Chicago passage is a two-sentence boosterish claim, and the UIC page is already the better-evidenced Chicago TIF account. No standalone page: the white paper is a 15-page Canva guide, mostly generic, with the useful content being the Transbay case, which the Tier 1 primaries cover better.
claim_grade: D (practitioner guidance / interpretive) with a few A-claims on the two cases that need the Tier 1 primaries below — source tier under §4c: Tier 2. ICLEI USA is the US arm of ICLEI, a membership association of local governments (a practitioner and advocacy body, climate-finance focus); the author is a staff adviser, not a scholar. The acknowledgements thank Dr David Merriman (UIC; co-author of the TIF-incidence literature the wiki's Walters page cites) 'for his peer review of this paper'. Peer review by a scholar does not lift the paper to Tier 1 and does not mean Merriman endorses the LVC framing; his own 2018 report says the opposite on that point (below).

content_summary.definition_of_tif_as_lvc: Page 6: TIF is 'a public financing tool that enables local governments to fund infrastructure, redevelopment, and other public projects by capturing the future increase in property tax revenues (the "increment") within a designated area'. Footnote 1a on page 6: 'TIFs are also at times referred to as "value capture." "Land Capture" [sic] is a broader term to include all mechanisms, such as TIF, development right sale, and strategic land management. Local improvement districts (LID) and Mello Roos Community Facility Districts, the latter which are limited to California, are a variant of TIF in that a new tax is imposed within the defined jurisdiction.' The paper's framing is 'capturing the value uplift' of public investment on ALL assessed property (land plus buildings); it never separates land value from improvement value and does not mention site-value taxation or the unearned increment. It also says TIFs 'are rarely, if ever, solely focused on GHG reductions, as such projects do not result in higher property valuations' (p. 6). Mechanics (pp. 6-7): base year, increment capture 'including from all governments (school districts, etc.)', pay-as-you-go versus bonds, fixed district life 'often 20-30 years'.
content_summary.legal_framework_summary: Page 8 (five bullets): state enabling legislation ('some form of TIF is allowed in almost every state'); public purpose requirement; notice and approval with public hearings and notice to affected taxing entities; equity and anti-displacement provisions ('Climate-related TIF districts risk gentrification; some states require affordable housing set-asides'); debt limitations (constitutional limits unless classed 'non-debt'). Some states require a 'but-for' analysis, 'intended to determine what would happen to property tax revenues in the absence of the TIF investment'. No statute is named and no state is compared.
content_summary.equity_and_displacement: Thin. Two sentences in total: the legal bullet above and, in 'Risks & Considerations' (p. 9), 'Equity Risks – Potential for displacement of low-income residents if climate improvements lead to rapid gentrification.' Other listed risks: revenue shortfall, legal challenges by property owners or school districts, market dependency. The paper does not discuss the rate-shift onto non-TIF taxpayers or school-district revenue loss, although its own definition notes the increment is taken from 'all governments (school districts, etc.)'. No data, no cases of displacement.
content_summary.bond_financing: Pages 6 and 10: bonds are normally sold up front and serviced from the increment; 'These bonds are most often backed by the full revenues of the issuing entity, as bondholders view the bonds backed solely by TIF revenues as risky'; TIF can supply a local match for federal or state grants; TIF 'may be applied more easily to climate resilience investments than to GHG reduction projects'. Lessons learned (p. 10): a project advocate in each stakeholder group, start from funding needs then set boundaries, strong cost-benefit analysis, careful district design, seek complementary funding.
content_summary.eight_steps: Pages 11-12: 1 Legal Review; 2 Project Identification; 3 Feasibility Study (analyse 'potential property value uplift'); 4 District Designation (boundaries, base year, term); 5 Stakeholder Engagement (overlapping taxing entities); 6 Financial Structuring (pay-as-you-go versus bonds, blend with grants and private investors); 7 Approval (vote or board adoption); 8 Implement, Monitoring & Reporting ('best practice to issue ongoing reporting on the project execution and actualized revenue gains'). Page headers on pp. 11-12 read 'FUNDING MUNICIPAL FLEET AND EQUIPMENT ELECTRIFICATION' — a template carry-over from another ICLEI paper.
content_summary.case_transbay_as_stated_by_iclei: Page 13: San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency 'used TIF to help finance the $4.2 billion Transbay Transit Center (also known as the Salesforce Transit Center)'; 'redeveloped 40 acres'; 'nine transportation systems under one roof'; the new tax revenues 'are captured through TIF and used to service debt payments on a $171 million' TIFIA loan; 'the first TIFIA loan secured by value capture revenues from real estate taxes on surrounding transit-oriented development'. Cited to the FHWA project profile (endnote 3).
content_summary.case_transbay_checked_against_tier1: FHWA Project Profile (official): sponsor and borrower is the Transbay Joint Powers Authority (created 2001; board includes the City and County of San Francisco, AC Transit and Caltrain), not SFMTA. Total programme cost estimate US$6,194 million; Phase 1 US$2,259.4 million (construction 1,488.9; programme costs 595.3; contingency 211.3). Phase 1 funding lines include land sales US$515.6 million (State), Transit Center District Plan Mello-Roos CFD US$146.6 million, TIFIA loan US$171 million, transferable development rights US$4 million, tolls and sales-tax lines. The TIFIA loan 'is secured by a senior lien on Project Revenues, which include dedicated tax increment revenues from land sold and developed in the state-owned parcels surrounding the Transit Center (98% of revenues)' plus AC Transit passenger-facilities charges (2%); credit agreement executed 25 January 2010; 'first TIFIA loan secured by value capture revenues from real estate taxes on surrounding transit oriented development' (confirms ICLEI's phrase). The area plan includes 2,600 new homes, 35% affordable. SF Controller's memo, 20 April 2020: in 2005 the Transbay Redevelopment Project Area was adopted 'to redevelop approximately 10 acres of property owned by the State of California' to fund the Transit Center; in 2012 the City adopted the Transit Center District Plan and authorised a Mello-Roos district; CFD No. 2014-1 formed 2014; 82.6 percent of CFD special tax goes to the train box and rooftop park; US$398.5 million of CFD special tax bonds issued; the TIFIA loan (up to US$171.0 million, 2010, fully drawn Dec 2016-Nov 2018, outstanding US$178.9 million on 1 Feb 2020) is repaid from net tax increment on certain State-owned parcels in the Transbay Redevelopment Area plus AC Transit contributions; an interim City Financing of up to US$260 million covered a roughly US$250 million Phase 1 shortfall after the 2015 MTC cost review; up to US$315 million of TJPA tax allocation bonds were authorised to refinance the TIFIA loan. Discrepancies with ICLEI: (a) the cost: FHWA's figures are US$2.26 billion for Phase 1 and US$6.19 billion for the programme, neither US$4.2 billion; (b) 'SFMTA' used TIF: the borrower and issuer is TJPA, with the City acting through the CFD and tax-allocation bonds; (c) '40 acres' is not in these sources, which give about 10 acres of state-owned parcels; (d) most important for a value-capture reading, the pledged increment comes from land the State owned and sold to developers (land sales alone were US$515.6 million in the FHWA table), so the case is largely public land disposal plus increment on that land, supplemented by a Mello-Roos special tax and a 2012 upzoning — not a freeze-and-divert of existing owners' tax base as in Chicago.
content_summary.case_chicago_as_stated_by_iclei: Page 13, headed 'B. Chicago, Illinois – Energy Efficiency District' but the text describes the city programme: 'over 100 TIF districts' used 'to promote economic and neighborhood development', allowing Chicago 'to leverage its public investment to attract over $6 billion in private capital investment in TIF districts'; projects include building energy retrofits, LED street lighting and commercial green roofs; revenue from the Central Loop TIF funds the Green Roof Improvement Fund. Endnotes cite the City of Chicago Office of Inspector General TIF map dashboard and the Adaptation Clearinghouse. The heading and text do not match (no 'Energy Efficiency District' is described), and the paper cites no evaluation of whether the $6 billion is TIF-caused. The IG dashboard page confirms only definitions (TIF district, fund balance, surplus) and that its dataset covers 2017 onward.
content_summary.chicago_tier1_anchors: The wiki's research/uic-chicago-tif-who-paid-who-gained.md (UIC Great Cities Institute, 26 August 2026; read in full, Tier 1) is the evidential anchor for Chicago: TIF raised citywide property-tax rates by an average 13.7 percent over 2014-2023 (18.6 percent by 2023), and on its preferred estimate only 1.8 percent of captured increment is attributable to TIF. That report post-dates ICLEI's July 2026 paper, which therefore does not engage it. The UIC study also bears on ICLEI's step 3 ('analyze potential property value uplift') and on the but-for test it mentions. Official primaries to locate for any Chicago factual sentence: the City of Chicago's annual TIF reports and Data Portal TIF dataset (not fetched) and the IG dashboard (fetched, definitions only).
content_summary.tier1_counterpoint_on_the_lvc_label: Merriman (2018), Lincoln Institute Policy Focus Report, section headed 'TIF Is Not Additional Land Value Capture' (printed p. 12): 'The property tax liability of property owners in TIF projects is the same as in projects using other funding mechanisms. Because of that, the general public "captures" no more of the value created by public investments in a TIF district than it would without the TIF district.' He adds that TIF subsidising private activity is 'more properly a device that "transfers" value to, rather than "captures" value from, the private sector', and (summary) that although results are mixed 'TIF often fails to meet its primary goal to increase real estate development and other economic growth'. This is the same scholar ICLEI thanks for peer review. The wiki's Walters (2012) page already reaches a compatible conclusion ('at best only a portion of a TIF increment qualifies as genuine LVC').
